# The Thirty-Seven Letters of Monk Hideo, As Compiled by His Opponent

---

## Editor's Preface

I will keep this brief because the letters themselves are not brief, and they have waited long enough.

My name is not important. Those who follow the old tournaments will know it. Those who do not will gain nothing from hearing it. What matters is that I am the man who, on the eleventh day of October in the forty-third year of Shōwa, was declared champion of the All-Japan Kendō Championship by forfeit, when my opponent in the final — Hideo Sakai, who had not lost a match in seven years of competition, who had dismantled the previous three rounds so cleanly that the judges' flags rose in unison before his opponents' shinai touched the floor — removed his men, placed his shinai on the court, bowed once, and walked out of the gymnasium. He was twenty-nine years old. Within the year he had entered a monastery in Tōhoku prefecture. Within two years all formal inquiries into the incident had been closed without finding cause for sanction or explanation.

I was twenty-six. I had won nothing.

Three months after the tournament, I received the first letter. Over the following forty years I received thirty-six more. I did not solicit them. I did not, for a long time, understand them. I am not certain I understand them now.

I am seventy years old and I have been told, in the particular language physicians reserve for conversations they would rather not have, that I will not see seventy-one. In the months this illness has given me to sit and consider what I still owe, I have returned again and again to these letters, which have lived in a cedar box in my study for as long as I have lived in this house. I have decided to make them public. I have arranged them in order and provided what contextual notes I am able to supply. Where Hideo's references are obscure, I have tried to clarify. Where his meaning is plain, I have not interfered.

I will say only that a match unfinished is a debt unpaid, and I have run out of years to owe.

I do not believe Hideo will object to this publication, though I have not asked him and do not know whether he is alive to be asked. The monastery has not responded to my last four letters. The abbot who had previously served as intermediary died in the winter of Heisei 22. It is possible that Hideo is dead. It is possible that he is not. In either case, his letters were sent to me, and they are mine to do with as I see fit.

I have kept them in their original envelopes. His calligraphy, particularly in the early years, was very fine.

— October, 2012

---

## I.

### Letter 1

*(Received January 14, 1969. Written on standard unlined paper. Envelope bears the monastery's address but no sender's name.)*

You will forgive me, I hope, for writing without invitation. Or perhaps you will not, and the letter will serve equally well as a stone thrown into water — the purpose is in the throwing, not in the reception.

I arrived here in the first week of November. The monastery sits in a valley between two mountains that the monks call, with a plainness I am still learning to admire, the left mountain and the right mountain. In winter the wind comes through the valley at such speeds that the wooden shutters must be latched by four in the afternoon or they will tear free. I have been assigned to latch them. It is work that requires no thought and much movement, and I suspect the assignment was made with my particular deficiencies in mind.

The days begin at half past three. By four we are in the meditation hall. I find that I am incapable of sitting still for the prescribed periods without considerable pain. The monks who have been here for years fold into their positions like cloth. I fold like rusted metal. But no one speaks of it, which I find more generous than encouragement would be.

The ink here freezes in its stone by mid-December. I am writing this quickly, before the cold takes the last of it.

I thought you should know that I am somewhere.

H.

---

*[Editor's note: I did not reply to this or to any of the first six letters. My reasons were not complicated. I did not know what to say. —Ed.]*

---

### Letter 2

*(Received March 3, 1969.)*

Spring is a rumor here. The older monks describe it with a reverence that suggests either genuine anticipation or an elaborate and longstanding joke at the expense of newcomers. I have been shown a plum tree, bare and blackened, and told it will bloom. I find this difficult to believe, but I have committed to a life of faith, so I will try.

I have been moved from shutters to the kitchen. The abbot believes, I think, that feeding others is a corrective for selfishness, though he has not said so directly. He communicates largely through the assignment of chores. A young monk who spoke too loudly during evening scripture was given sole charge of the henhouse for three months. He is now the quietest man in the compound. The hens are, by contrast, unbearable.

I mention this because it strikes me that you, too, were always someone who communicated through action rather than speech. I remember this about you, though we exchanged very few words. One communicates a great deal in a match without speaking. You carried your shinai in your left hand before each bout and transferred it only at the line. I never asked whether this was superstition or habit. It is strange, the things one retains.

H.

---

### Letter 3

*(Received August 19, 1969.)*

Summer here is a violence. The insects alone could constitute an invading army. We sleep with netting that the oldest monks repair by hand, their fingers working in the dark with a precision that I can only describe as martial, though they would reject the comparison.

There is a monk here — I will call him K., though that is not his name or initial — whose hands shake when he performs calligraphy. He came to the monastery in his twentieth year, from what life I do not know. The abbot has him copy sutras every afternoon. His tremor is pronounced. The characters, as a result, have an appearance of agitation on the page, as though the words themselves are distressed by their content. And yet: he has been copying sutras for thirty-one years, and his hand still shakes. The body remembers what the mind has released. I find this either a comfort or a terror, depending on the hour.

I have not asked K. about his life before the monastery. It is understood here that one's previous life is a separate country, and we do not issue visas.

I trust you are well. I ask this knowing I will not receive an answer, which is perhaps why I can ask it honestly.

H.

---

### Letter 4

*(Received February 2, 1970.)*

Another winter. The ink has frozen again. I have learned to keep the inkstone beneath my robes during meditation, warming it against my body. This is technically a violation of posture and probably of spirit, but the abbot has seen me do it and said nothing, which here passes for permission.

I have begun, in the hours between evening meal and sleep, to read. The monastery's library is small but has depth in unexpected places. Someone, decades ago, donated a nearly complete collection of Takuan Sōhō's letters. I have been reading his correspondence with Yagyū Munenori — the sword-priest writing to the sword-master — and finding in it a strange mirror. Takuan left the world to enter religion and then spent decades writing to the men who remained in the world of blades. One leaves a thing and spends one's life describing the shape of its absence. Perhaps that is what religion is. A practice of structured absence.

I do not know why I am telling you this. I continue to write to you as one continues to face a direction long after the landmark has disappeared — out of an orientation that has become structural.

H.

---

*[Editor's note: The four letters reproduced above constitute the earliest phase of the correspondence. Letters 5 and 6, received in 1970 and early 1971 respectively, are similar in character: descriptions of monastic routine, seasonal observations, brief literary references. Neither mentions the tournament or the events of October 1968. Both are addressed, as all subsequent letters would be, in the formal second person, to me. I have omitted them in the interest of space but can attest to their consistency of tone. I replied for the first time in March of 1971. My letter was short and concerned, if I recall correctly, the weather. —Ed.]*

---

## II.

### Letter 7

*(Received May 15, 1971.)*

Your letter arrived yesterday. I read it four times, which is three more times than its content strictly warranted, unless one considers the weather in the southern prefectures to be a matter of deep philosophical significance, which perhaps it is, and I have simply not yet advanced far enough in my training to perceive it.

I am glad you wrote. That is all I will say on the subject.

A thing has happened that I want to describe to you precisely, because you are the only person I know who would understand its significance. During morning training — we do not practice martial arts here, but the physical labor of the monastery has its own forms, its own geometries — I was carrying water from the well to the kitchen. Two buckets on a pole across the shoulders. The path is uneven. The weight shifts. And I found my body making a correction — a rotation of the rear hip to absorb the imbalance — that I recognized. It was not a movement I learned here. It was a movement from *before*. My body, under strain, returned to its oldest training. I set down the buckets and stood in the path for some time.

I mention this not out of nostalgia but out of a growing suspicion that there are forms of knowledge that do not answer to the will. The mind renounces. The body retains. I am beginning to think that the project of this life — the monastic project, the project of release — is not the elimination of such knowledge but the slow, patient negotiation with it. One does not empty the cup. One learns to hold the cup without drinking.

But I wonder, sometimes, whether it is more dangerous to hold what one will not use than to use what one holds.

H.

---

### Letter 9

*(Received January 8, 1972.)*

I have been thinking about obligation.

The Hagakure tells us that the way of the warrior is found in death — that one must rehearse one's death each morning and each evening, so that when the moment arrives the body does not flinch. But Yamamoto also tells us that loyalty to one's lord supersedes loyalty to one's own honor, and here I find a knot I cannot untie.

Consider a case. Not a real case — a hypothetical, of the kind we might set for students. A warrior serves a lord. In the course of his service, he comes to know something about the lord — not a moral failing, not a sin, but a *weakness*. A gap in the lord's armor that the lord himself cannot see. The warrior knows that if this weakness is exploited by an enemy, the lord will die. He knows equally that if he informs the lord, the knowledge itself may undo the lord — that to know one is vulnerable is sometimes to *become* vulnerable in a way that far exceeds the original flaw. What is the warrior's duty?

The Hagakure would say: speak, and accept the consequences. Loyalty demands honesty.

But I have come to believe that the Hagakure was written by a man who did not sufficiently appreciate the violence of honesty — its capacity to destroy the very thing it claims to protect.

I set this question before you as one sets a stone on a go board: not to win, but to see what shape the game takes.

H.

---

*[Editor's note: Letter 8, omitted here, is a brief seasonal description of autumn at the monastery and contains no material bearing on the themes of the collection. —Ed.]*

---

### Letter 12

*(Received November 3, 1974.)*

You ask, in your last letter, whether I am describing a real situation or merely exercising my mind on abstractions.

I deflect the question, but not because the answer is unclear to me. Rather, I am not certain the distinction matters. A hypothetical, if it is sufficiently close to the bone, becomes a confession by other means. And a confession, if it is sufficiently abstract, becomes merely a hypothetical with pretensions. We circle each other, you and I, as we always have.

But let me tighten the circle.

Imagine two swordsmen. They have trained in the same tradition, or in traditions proximate enough that each can read the other's form as fluently as his own handwriting. They are to fight. In the days or hours before the bout, one of them perceives in the other's technique a flaw — not a lapse of discipline, not a failure of training, but a structural fault, a thing bred into the bone by ten thousand repetitions of a stance that was, unbeknownst to the practitioner, fractionally wrong from the very first lesson. The flaw is invisible to the man who carries it. It may be invisible to every other opponent he will face. But to this one swordsman, at this one moment, it is as legible as a character written in fire.

What does that swordsman owe?

If he fights, he will win, because the flaw is mortal. The corridor it opens is narrow but absolute. He will win, and his opponent will know that he lost but will not know *why*, and will carry that unknowing forward into every subsequent bout, where the flaw waits like a crack in a bridge — invisible until the weight comes.

If he speaks, he will save his opponent's life — possibly, eventually, literally — but he will also unmake his opponent's understanding of himself as a swordsman. Every victory the opponent has ever won becomes suspect. Every match,  in retrospect, becomes a match he might have lost had his opponent possessed the same knowledge. The flaw retroactively contaminates the entire history.

If he does neither — if he refuses both combat and disclosure —

But here I stop, because the third option requires a sacrifice that I am not yet prepared to describe in the abstract. The abstract has begun to fray.

I trust your autumn has been mild.

H.

---

*[Editor's note: I should mention that Hideo's letters did not arrive in a vacuum. I was, during these years, an active instructor and competitor. I had won the All-Japan championship three more times after 1968 — in 1970, 1973, and 1975 — and was widely regarded as the foremost kendōka of my generation. The letters arrived, were read, were placed in the box, and life continued. I do not say this to diminish them. I say it because the reader should understand that the letters existed alongside an ordinary life, and that ordinary life has its own gravity.]*

*[I should also mention that I replied to nearly all of the letters from this period, though my replies were not, I think, what Hideo was looking for. I wrote about my students, about tournament results, about technical developments in the practice. I did not engage with the hypotheticals. I did not feel qualified to. —Ed.]*

### Letter 14

*(Received June 22, 1976.)*

Your letter about the Nagoya regional tournament arrived. I was pleased to hear about your student Yamashiro's performance. A clean kote in the semifinal is not a small thing, particularly against a left-handed opponent. You describe his development with obvious pride and with the technical eye that I have always — you will permit me — admired.

But you did not address my question, and you have not addressed my questions for some time now, and I am beginning to wonder whether your silence on these matters is its own form of answer.

I will set out the dilemma one more time, in a different frame.
